analysis.one_liner: Automatically subjects the largest nonbank financial firms to strict bank-style oversight and creates a panel to study climate risk to the financial system.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2020, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 crisis, regulators were supposed to designate big nonbank financial companies—insurers, hedge fund and asset managers—for extra oversight, but in practice very few ever were. This bill would make that automatic: any nonbank firm above set size thresholds would immediately be subject to tougher capital requirements, stress tests, and wind-down plans, unless regulators specifically voted to exempt it. It would also give the Financial Stability Oversight Council power to regulate risky financial activities directly, create a subcommittee to study how climate change threatens the financial system, and require the oversight council to be better staffed, better funded, and meet partly in public.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit indirectly: stricter oversight of the largest financial firms reduces the odds of a 2008-style crisis, where failures at lightly regulated nonbank companies spread through the economy and taxpayers were asked to fund bailouts. The climate-risk subcommittee and public meeting requirements also give the public more visibility into how regulators watch the financial system. The direct beneficiaries of stronger rules are households and small businesses that bear the cost of financial crashes.

how_it_helps.text: It automatically designates very large nonbank financial companies as systemically important, subjecting them to capital and liquidity rules, annual stress tests, and 'living wills' plans for winding down without a taxpayer rescue.
It gives the Financial Stability Oversight Council power to step in and regulate any activity or practice that threatens the financial system if the primary regulator fails to act within 12 months.
It creates a Climate Change Subcommittee within the Council to annually assess the risk climate change poses to financial stability.

It requires minimum staffing and funding for the Council and the Office of Financial Research (at least 75 Council staff, 300 OFR staff, and $168 million a year in industry assessments), and requires at least one Council meeting each quarter to be open to the public with transcripts released.

analysis.who_pays: Large nonbank financial companies—big insurers, private fund and asset managers, and other financial firms above the bill's size thresholds—would bear the cost of higher capital buffers, stress tests, and stricter supervision. Those costs could partly be passed on to customers through higher fees or tighter credit.

drawbacks.text: Bright-line thresholds (for example, $50 billion in assets or $1.5 trillion under management) can be arbitrary: firms just above the line escape oversight while firms just below it face the cost of complying, and firms may restructure to stay under the thresholds.

The tougher capital, liquidity, and stress-test standards the bill triggers cost regulated firms money, and some of that cost can be passed on to borrowers and investors through slightly higher prices or lower returns—though the 2008 crisis showed the cost of inadequate oversight of these same firms is far larger.

The automatic designation plus the Council's new power to regulate any 'risky activity' concentrates substantial discretionary power in a small body of regulators, which opponents of financial regulation argue can chill lending or misjudge which activities are actually risky.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—keeping the 2008 pattern of large nonbank firms escaping tough oversight from recurring, and putting climate risk on the regulatory map—are broad and mostly borne by a narrow group of large financial firms. The main drawbacks are compliance costs that could be passed on to consumers, and the risk that bright-line size thresholds (like the $50 billion asset line) create perverse incentives or catch firms by surprise. The bill also concentrates significant new rulemaking power in one council of regulators, which critics could fairly call an accountability trade-off. On the whole it is a modest, well-targeted strengthening of existing law rather than a radical overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuy Garcia introduced the bill on April 14, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Its core provisions—automatic designation of large nonbank firms, Council rulemaking authority, minimum staffing and funding, public meetings, and a climate risk subcommittee—were never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large nonbank financial companies avoided automatic strict oversight, and no firm faces the capital, stress-test, or climate-risk requirements this bill would have imposed.

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its main provisions on April 14, 2020.

for.name: 9 of 231 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Porter, Grijalva, Schakowsky, McGovern, Norton, Danny K. Davis, and others)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members ever added support.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral—no markup, no vote, no report—so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Large nonbank financial firms and asset managers
against.what_they_did: The industries that would have faced new capital, stress-test, and supervision requirements are the consistent, well-documented opponents of expanded designation authority; no industry support for the bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced out of the Democratic-majority committee either.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (insurers, asset managers, hedge funds)
industries.note: Firms above the bill's size thresholds would automatically face Fed supervision, capital and liquidity rules, stress tests, and living wills—costs they avoided after regulators declined to designate them. Ordinary people benefit because these firms' failures helped cause the 2008 crisis and bailouts.

Banks were already subject to similar prudential standards; the bill mainly adds the Council as a backstop that can force any regulator to act on risky practices, slightly shifting power toward the centralized council and away from individual agencies.

industries.industry: Office of Financial Research and Council staff (federal financial regulators)
industries.note: The bill guarantees these oversight agencies minimum funding and staffing and data access from member agencies, entrenching the government's capacity to monitor Wall Street. It also opens one Council meeting per quarter to the public and requires released transcripts.
